shows.title: What the Land Remembers — Counter-Archives from Iran
shows.artist: Sara Abbasnejad, Sana Ahmadizadeh, Ghazel, Mohammad Hassanzadeh, Anahita Hekmat, Minoo Iranpour, Simin Keramati, Mina Keshavarz, Golriz Kolahi, Anahita Norouzi, Neda Razavipour, Sanaz Sohrabi, Morteza Soorani, Sadegh Tirafkan
shows.description:
Built around the Parking Video Library, an independent counter-archive of Iranian film and video founded in Tehran in 2004 by artist and curator Amirali Ghasemi, this exhibition assembles two decades of moving-image work made under conditions of censorship and scarcity. Rather than a survey of Iranian art history, it treats the archive itself as the subject: rediscovered tapes, early digital experiments, and rarely screened installations are presented as evidence of how artists kept recording when official channels tried to erase them.

The material is organized into two loose constellations. One looks back to the 1990s and early 2000s, restaging the makeshift, resourceful conditions under which artists worked in the aftermath of war. The other, focused on Iran's southwestern oil region, gathers contemporary pieces that trace the ecological and geopolitical fallout of extraction and conflict in that landscape. Across both, film, video, photography and installation sit alongside one another as different strategies for preserving testimony.

Coming at a moment of renewed conflict and internet blackouts affecting Iran, the show has an unusually urgent framing: every image here is presented as something that could easily have been lost. For a Brussels audience, it's a rare chance to see Iranian experimental and documentary practice not filtered through a single canonical narrative but through the messier, more personal record of an archive built outside institutions.

shows.title: Là où marchent les dieux
shows.description:
Abel Burger works in a private, almost devotional register: thick, chalky layers of mixed media on paper and wood build up figures and totems that feel excavated rather than drawn, as if unearthed from some imagined ancient culture. Faces dissolve into masks, bodies fuse with architecture, and gold-brown grounds give the whole body of work the patina of relics rather than contemporary drawings.

This solo show, whose title translates as "where the gods walk," continues Burger's long-running interest in personal mythology — invented rites, ancestor figures, and archaeologies of feeling that borrow the visual language of icons and reliquaries without belonging to any real religion. Recurring motifs like leviathans, arches, and robed figures suggest a private cosmology built up work by work over years.

Burger, who lives and works on the French Mediterranean coast, has shown steadily with Galerie DYS and at fairs like Drawing Now Paris; this exhibition gathers new works on paper and panel alongside pieces that trace how her vocabulary of pale bodies and gilded grounds has developed. It rewards slow looking — these are quiet, dense pictures built for close reading rather than a quick pass through the gallery.

shows.title: Soleil Noir
shows.description:
The Villa Empain's autumn exhibition puts Léon Spilliaert, the great solitary draughtsman of Belgian symbolism, into dialogue with the artists who shaped and followed him — James Ensor at one end, Michaël Borremans at the other. Spilliaert's ink-and-watercolor nocturnes, all those empty seafronts and self-portraits staring back in mirrors, tend to reward exactly the kind of close, quiet looking the Villa Empain's rooms are suited to.

Details on the full checklist aren't yet public, but pairing Spilliaert with contemporaries and later Belgian painters suggests a show interested in tracing a specific, melancholic strain of Belgian art across a century rather than a straight monograph.

This one is still a few weeks out from opening; check back closer to October for full details on works and layout.

shows.title: François Delfosse
shows.description:
This is the gallery's next scheduled show, running about a month in the small Ixelles space that Didier Devillez has run for decades on a tight roster of Belgian painters, sculptors and writers. Delfosse's own images — the handful posted to the gallery's site — suggest figurative, textured paintings, in keeping with the gallery's long-standing focus on figuration and expressionist-leaning work.

Didier Devillez has been showing largely the same core group of artists since the gallery's founding, mounting six to eight exhibitions a year alongside talks and studio visits, so a Delfosse show here places him in company with the gallery's other represented painters and writers rather than as part of a themed group exhibition.

Full checklist and press details weren't posted at the time of writing; worth a look for anyone tracking the more old-guard, unhurried end of the Brussels gallery scene.

shows.title: I am not me, the horse is not mine
shows.description:
William Kentridge takes over Bozar as its first "Grand Invité," a season-long residency built around a single large exhibition rather than a conventional one-off show. At its center is his theatrical practice — the charcoal drawings, stop-motion animations, and torn-paper collages that Kentridge films and refilms to build his signature moving-image works, alongside the sculptural props, puppets, and "studio objects" that populate his films and stage productions.

Kentridge's work circles obsessively around history's unfinished business: colonialism, apartheid-era South Africa, revolution and its betrayals, staged through a very physical, hand-made animation technique of drawing, erasing, and redrawing on the same sheet of paper. Expect large-scale charcoal drawings related to films like "The Refusal of Time" and "The Great Yes, The Great No," alongside props and objects from his stage and opera work, including pieces connected to his production of Alban Berg's "Wozzeck" and other theatrical collaborations.

The exhibition is the anchor of a much wider Bozar program built around Kentridge this season — concerts, an "Open air cinema" of his short films, and events with his Johannesburg workshop, the Centre for the Less Good Idea — making this less a single show than an extended residency by one of the most theatrically minded artists working today.

shows.title: Jean Brusselmans: Painter by Nature
shows.description:
This is the first full retrospective in nearly fifty years of Jean Brusselmans (1884-1953), a Belgian painter who spent his career at a deliberate remove from Paris and the avant-gardes, building a stubborn, geometric style out of the Brabant countryside around him. Around 120 paintings and works on paper trace how his early, darker figuration hardened over decades into flattened, almost tessellated landscapes and interiors — fields, kitchen tables, and family portraits reduced to blocks of muted color locked together like a puzzle.

The show places Brusselmans in conversation with contemporaries such as Fernand Léger, Piet Mondrian, and Rik Wouters, which helps explain a painter who absorbed cubism and abstraction's lessons about structure without ever quite leaving the visible world behind. A side gallery revives his forgotten set designs for the 1936 Brussels premiere of Schoenberg's opera "Erwartung," reconstructed through new work by contemporary painter Kristof Santy — a nice reminder that this quiet, undersung modernist also worked, briefly, for the stage.

For a painter so tied to a specific patch of Belgian ground, and so long overshadowed by his internationally minded peers, this is a rare chance to see the full arc of his work assembled in one place.

shows.title: The Fabric Decides
shows.description:
This small, focused exhibition stages an unlikely conversation between Belgian artist Edith Dekyndt, known for sculptural and process-based work with unstable materials — dust, light, oxidised metal, tension — and rarely-shown archival pieces from couturier Cristóbal Balenciaga. Both practices, it turns out, are obsessed with the same question: what a piece of fabric remembers, and how cloth holds the trace of a gesture or a body long after the hand that shaped it has moved on.

Dekyndt has spent years making work from materials that shift, decay, or respond to their environment, and here that sensibility is set directly against haute couture construction — Balenciaga's structural, sculptural approach to fabric, famous for holding its shape almost independent of the body wearing it. The pairing is less a fashion exhibition than a material-studies exercise, tracing how skill, memory, and time are embedded in textiles across two very different disciplines.

It's an intimate show by Bozar's standards, staged in the museum's smaller Antichambres galleries, and it rewards a slow, close look at surface and construction rather than a survey approach.

shows.title: Romina Remmo
shows.description:
Romina Remmo works with thread the way a painter works with pigment. Trained as a photographer as well as an embroiderer, she has spent years developing a vocabulary built from filament, lace, and stitched fabric, materials traditionally coded as domestic and feminine that she redirects toward much darker territory. Pieces built from lingerie, garter belts, and delicate lacework sit alongside titles referencing explosive devices and packages, an unsettling collision that runs through much of her practice.

This solo exhibition at Zedes, opening as part of the gallery's autumn program, brings together a new body of work continuing Remmo's long-running exploration of textile as a carrier of memory, desire, and violence. Her pieces often read initially as sensuous or ornamental before their titles or details recast them as something more confrontational, a strategy that has made her one of the more distinctive voices working in fiber and mixed media in Belgium today.

Visitors familiar with Remmo's photography and earlier embroidered works will find her continuing to push at the boundary between seduction and threat, using needle and thread as tools of both intimacy and unease.

shows.title: La part du signe
shows.description:
Bertrand Flachot's residency at Odradek's Saint-Gilles space centers on drawing pushed to the edge of language. His linear, cursive marks drift between figuration and abstraction, recalling handwriting that has come loose from any fixed alphabet — lines that behave like sentences without quite settling into words. Photography and installation extend that same wandering logic into the room itself, so the works read less as discrete objects than as a continuous, unfolding gesture.

The show sits at the meeting point of drawing and writing that has interested artists loosely associated with Belgium's Cobra and post-Cobra circles for decades — the mark as both image and sign — but Flachot's version feels quieter and more exploratory, closer to a private notational system than a public statement. Seen in the intimate rooms of Odradek's residency space, the work rewards slow looking: what first reads as pure abstraction gradually resolves into rhythms that feel almost legible, then dissolves again.

shows.title: Eight Sculptures
shows.dates_note: Venue's "Current" exhibitions page lists this show with no exact dates; homepage states gallery reopens for the season with "Next vernissage on Sunday 6 September, 2026."
shows.description:
Seyni Awa Camara, the self-taught Senegalese sculptor who died earlier this year, worked clay with her bare hands, without sketches or armatures, letting each form emerge directly from the material rather than from a preconceived plan. This selection of eight terracotta sculptures brings together three of her large protective figures — including a densely populated maternity scene and two hybrid, totemic creatures — alongside five smaller works drawn from everyday life, mixing domestic animals with modes of transport.

Camara's process was as physical as it was intuitive: pieces were fired outdoors in open pits, pulled out red-hot, and plunged into a fermented plant bath that fixed their characteristic dark, reddish patina. Her recurring motifs — two-headed bodies, figures loaded with children, faces of blank, frontal intensity — grew out of her own experience of difficult maternities in Diola culture, where fertility carries heavy social weight; she reworked the protective kagnalène rite into a private visual language.

Camara's international recognition dates to her inclusion in the landmark 1989 Centre Pompidou exhibition Magiciens de la terre, after which her work entered major public and private collections without her ever leaving her home in Bignona, Casamance. This small, focused presentation offers a rare chance to see her sculpture at close range in Brussels.

shows.title: Resonance / Dialogue
shows.dates_note: Venue's "Current" exhibitions page lists this show with no exact dates; homepage states gallery reopens for the season with "Next vernissage on Sunday 6 September, 2026."
shows.description:
For his third solo outing at Rossicontemporary, Ghent-based sculptor Johan De Wit shows two related bodies of work: his "Cupboards" — dressers crowded with hundreds of hand-formed bottles, pots and vessels — and wall-based "canvases" built from folded and curled surfaces. Both treat sculpture as a pictorial act: the dressers read like a three-dimensional still life, dense and orderly yet fragile, while the wall pieces trade the flatness of painting for a rippled, light-catching relief.

De Wit's palette owes an evident debt to the Old Masters, from the Flemish Primitives through to Morandi, and he mixes his own pigments from natural earths, ochres and ground minerals to get colour that seems to sit inside the material rather than on top of it. The sculptures start from a lightweight paper armature built up with resin and marble and iron powder, hand-shaped while drying so that each piece sags and settles unrepeatably.

The effect he's after is a minimalism that never goes cold: simplified, memory-built forms — pots, boxes, paintings — handled with enough tactility and imperfection that they feel alive rather than resolved.

shows.title: Sabbeteur des images
shows.dates_note: Venue's "Current" exhibitions page lists this show with no exact dates; homepage states gallery reopens for the season with "Next vernissage on Sunday 6 September, 2026."
shows.description:
For his first solo show at Rossicontemporary, Belgian artist Randoald Sabbe presents a broad, playful selection of text paintings, object assemblages and repurposed signage under the manifesto-like title Sabbeteur des images. Since 2020 he has built a practice out of hijacking ordinary visual material — commercial signs, popular references, everyday accessories, familiar sayings — and turning it back on the viewer as a kind of riddle.

The work sits in the gap between language and image, concealing as much as it reveals: pieces suggest rather than state, leaving the visitor to do the work of interpretation. Underneath the humour is a sustained interest in how history, politics and belief get encoded into the throwaway graphics of daily life.

It's a lighter, more mischievous register than much of what the gallery shows, but no less pointed — art that uses the vernacular of signage and slogan to needle at bigger questions about memory, meaning and shared reference.

shows.title: Congé de maternité
shows.dates_note: Venue's "Current" exhibitions page lists this show with no exact dates; homepage states gallery reopens for the season with "Next vernissage on Sunday 6 September, 2026."
shows.description:
After several years away from the gallery circuit, Carolina Fernández returns to Rossicontemporary with a dozen new oil paintings made since becoming a mother. Congé de maternité treats that transition not as a pause in her practice but as its own new territory — a way of looking at the world again, as if for the first time, through the disrupted rhythms of caregiving.

The paintings mix scenes of domestic life with memories of her Colombian childhood: toys, baby monitors, paper cutouts and stickers sit alongside the animal figures — dogs, Elizabethan collars — that have long populated her work as symbols of illness, healing and dependence on others. The result is a loose, direct kind of figuration, painted in the scraps of time available between feedings and naps rather than in extended studio sessions.

Fernández trained formally in fine art, and it shows in the handling — sensitive, detailed, quietly symbolic — even as the subject matter stays resolutely unglamorous. Between the ordered calm of her adopted Belgium and the more exuberant memory of Colombia, the show reads as a meditation on transmission, resilience and what gets carried forward.

shows.title: The Parliament of the Pitiful
shows.description:
The Parliament of the Pitiful is Laura Vandewynckel's opening exhibition at Pilar, the VUB's house of art and science on the Etterbeek campus. Details of the work itself are sparse on the venue's own listing beyond the title and format, but the name promises a gathering of abject or overlooked figures assembled into something like a mock political body — a premise that suits Pilar's habit of mixing visual art with its wider music, film and performance programme under one roof.

Pilar operates less like a conventional gallery and more like a cultural clubhouse embedded in a university campus, and exhibitions there tend to sit alongside concerts, film nights and talks rather than standing alone. This show is worth catching for visitors curious to see how a young Belgian artist uses the language of parliamentary assembly and pity to build a room-filling installation.
